analysis.investment_thesis: Anup Engineering is a genuinely good business with ROIC of ~22-25%, but at ~4.1% earnings yield (EBIT/EV), it fails the Magic Formula's cheapness test decisively. The market has already priced in the quality, leaving little margin of safety for new buyers.
key_strengths: ROIC ~22-25% (EBIT 168 Cr / Capital Employed ~665 Cr) — clears the 20% quality threshold
Revenue and profit compounding at 24.5% and 22.4% CAGR respectively over 5 years — rare in industrials
Low leverage (D/E 0.25) with operating margins expanding from 28% to 31% of operating income on revenue base
key_risks: Earnings yield ~4.1% (EBIT 168 Cr / EV ~4,105 Cr) — well below the 6% floor; P/E of 34.8x leaves no margin of safety
Operating CF turned sharply negative in FY2025 (-7 Cr) despite INR 118 Cr net profit — severe working capital deterioration
FCF negative two of last three years (-45 Cr in FY2023, -51 Cr in FY2025); capital-intensive growth cycle compressing free cash returns
red_flags: Operating CF of -7 Cr in FY2025 against net profit of 118 Cr implies massive working capital build or earnings quality concern
Gross margin reported at 3.79% is anomalously low vs 17.9% operating margin — data inconsistency warrants scrutiny
Borrowings jumped to 158 Cr yet Total Debt shows 32 Cr — unexplained discrepancy in balance sheet classification
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Running the Magic Formula: EBIT for FY2025 is INR 168 Cr (operating income). Enterprise Value = Market Cap (4,076 Cr) + Net Debt (32 - 3 = 29 Cr) ≈ 4,105 Cr. Earnings Yield = 168/4,105 = 4.1% — significantly below the 6% minimum and nowhere near the 12%+ that would make Greenblatt excited. ROIC = EBIT / (Equity 636 + Debt 32 - Cash 3) ≈ 168/665 = 25.3%, which clears the 20% quality bar. So Anup passes one test (quality) but fails the other (price). The Magic Formula demands both; the market has fully priced this quality premium in.

The FY2025 cash flow is a serious concern: a company reporting INR 118 Cr net profit generating -7 Cr operating cash and -51 Cr FCF is absorbing cash somewhere — likely long order-book cycles creating receivable/inventory bloat typical in capital goods. While the 24.5% revenue CAGR and 22.4% profit CAGR are impressive, and the order pipeline from oil & gas, chemicals, and hydrogen capex is structurally supportive, the current valuation (EV/EBITDA 22.4x, P/E 34.8x) demands perfect execution. At roughly 4% earnings yield, the Magic Formula screener would rank this in the bottom quartile on value — a Hold at best until earnings yield approaches 8-10%.
